objective: Theoretical probability = number of favorable outcomes / total number of outcomes, for discrete sample spaces where all outcomes equally likely.；Three-set Venn diagram: probability of single set, union, intersection, complement can be calculated using area counts.；Mutually exclusive events: P(A∪B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A∩B). If P(A∩B)=0, events are mutually exclusive.

learningGoals.statement: Students can calculate theoretical probability for discrete sample spaces with equally likely outcomes.
Students can calculate probabilities using three-set Venn diagrams, including unions, intersections, and complements.
Students can verify whether events are mutually exclusive using the formula P(A∪B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A∩B).

knowledgeNodes.name: Theoretical Probability
knowledgeNodes.definition: The ratio of the number of favorable outcomes to the total number of equally likely outcomes in a discrete sample space.
knowledgeNodes.ossdExpectation: Determine the theoretical probability, Pi (i.e., a value from 0 to 1), of each outcome of a discrete sample space (e.g., in situations in which all outcomes are equally likely), recognize that the sum of the probabilities of the outcomes is 1 (i.e., for n outcomes, P1 + P2 + P3 + … + Pn = 1), recognize that the probabilities Pi form the probability distribution associated with the sample space, and solve related problems.

knowledgeNodes.name: Three-Set Venn Diagram Probability
knowledgeNodes.definition: Using a Venn diagram with three overlapping sets to calculate probabilities of single sets, unions, intersections, and complements based on region counts.
knowledgeNodes.ossdExpectation: Recognize and describe an event as a set of outcomes and as a subset of a sample space, determine the complement of an event, determine whether two or more events are mutually exclusive or non-mutually exclusive (e.g., the events of getting an even number or getting an odd number of heads from tossing a coin 5 times are mutually exclusive), and solve related probability problems [e.g., calculate P(~A), P(A and B), P(A or B)] using a variety of strategies.

knowledgeNodes.name: Mutually Exclusive Events
knowledgeNodes.definition: Events are mutually exclusive if they cannot occur simultaneously; verified by P(A∩B)=0. The formula P(A∪B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A∩B) is used.
knowledgeNodes.ossdExpectation: Recognize and describe an event as a set of outcomes and as a subset of a sample space, determine the complement of an event, determine whether two or more events are mutually exclusive or non-mutually exclusive (e.g., the events of getting an even number or getting an odd number of heads from tossing a coin 5 times are mutually exclusive), and solve related probability problems [e.g., calculate P(~A), P(A and B), P(A or B)] using a variety of strategies.

questions.stem: If you roll a standard 6‑sided die, what is the theoretical probability of rolling a number greater than 4?
questions.successCriteria: Student correctly identifies 2 favorable outcomes (5 and 6) and calculates 2/6 = 1/3.
questions.ossdExpectation: Determine the theoretical probability, Pi (i.e., a value from 0 to 1), of each outcome of a discrete sample space (e.g., in situations in which all outcomes are equally likely), recognize that the sum of the probabilities of the outcomes is 1 (i.e., for n outcomes, P1 + P2 + P3 + … + Pn = 1), recognize that the probabilities Pi form the probability distribution associated with the sample space, and solve related problems.
questions.alignmentNote: Question directly assesses theoretical probability calculation as per SE A1.3 and aligns with OE A1 node.
questions.stemIntent: Check if student can apply the definition of theoretical probability to a simple dice scenario.
questions.commonMisconception: Student may incorrectly count favorable outcomes (e.g., only one number greater than 4) or include 4 itself.

options.label: A
options.feedbackWrong: 1/6 would be the probability of rolling a single specific number, not numbers greater than 4.

options.label: B
options.feedbackCorrect: Correct. The numbers greater than 4 are 5 and 6 (2 favorable outcomes out of 6 total), so the probability is 2/6 = 1/3.

options.label: C
options.feedbackWrong: 1/2 would be correct if 3 out of 6 outcomes were favorable, but here only 2 are favorable.

options.label: D
options.feedbackWrong: 2/3 would require 4 favorable outcomes out of 6, but only 2 are favorable.

questions.stem: From a standard 52-card deck, let event A be drawing a heart and event B be drawing a king. Are events A and B mutually exclusive?
questions.successCriteria: Student recognizes that P(A∩B) ≠ 0 (king of hearts) and therefore events are not mutually exclusive.
questions.ossdExpectation: Recognize and describe an event as a set of outcomes and as a subset of a sample space, determine the complement of an event, determine whether two or more events are mutually exclusive or non-mutually exclusive (e.g., the events of getting an even number or getting an odd number of heads from tossing a coin 5 times are mutually exclusive), and solve related probability problems [e.g., calculate P(~A), P(A and B), P(A or B)] using a variety of strategies.
questions.alignmentNote: Question requires analyzing whether two events are mutually exclusive, directly matching SE A1.5.
questions.stemIntent: Check if student can determine mutual exclusivity by considering whether the events can occur together.
questions.commonMisconception: Student thinks that because something is a heart and also a king are different categories, they cannot happen together; or that drawing a king always excludes hearts.

options.label: A
options.feedbackWrong: Actually, the king of hearts belongs to both events, so P(A∩B) = 1/52, not 0.

options.label: B
options.feedbackCorrect: Correct. The king of hearts is both a heart and a king, so the intersection is non-empty; events are not mutually exclusive.

options.label: C
options.text: Yes, because they are different suits
options.feedbackWrong: Different suits do not guarantee mutual exclusivity; a card can be both a heart and a king.

options.label: D
options.text: No, because P(A∪B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A∩B) is not zero
options.feedbackWrong: The formula itself is always true; mutual exclusivity is determined by whether P(A∩B)=0, not by the union sum being zero.

questions.stem:
Two-way table of elementary students' goals:

|            | Popular | Sports | Good Grades |
|------------|---------|--------|-------------|
| Female     | 30      | 30     | 40          |
| Male       | 20      | 10     | 20          |

What is the probability that a student who is female chose Sports?
questions.successCriteria: Student correctly identifies the base (all females) and calculates 30/100.
questions.ossdExpectation: Determine the theoretical probability, Pi (i.e., a value from 0 to 1), of each outcome of a discrete sample space (e.g., in situations in which all outcomes are equally likely), recognize that the sum of the probabilities of the outcomes is 1 (i.e., for n outcomes, P1 + P2 + P3 + … + Pn = 1), recognize that the probabilities Pi form the probability distribution associated with the sample space, and solve related problems.
questions.alignmentNote: Conditional probability here requires theoretical probability from a subset of the sample space, aligning with SE A1.3.
questions.stemIntent: Check if student can compute a conditional probability by correctly restricting the sample space to the condition (female).
questions.commonMisconception: Student uses total sample space as denominator (150) or uses the intersection of female and sports over total sports (30/40).

options.label: A
options.feedbackCorrect: Correct. There are 100 females total, and 30 of them chose Sports.

options.label: B
options.feedbackWrong: 30/150 would be the probability that a random student is female and chose Sports, not the conditional probability given female.

options.label: C
options.feedbackWrong: 30/40 uses total number of students who chose Sports (40) as denominator; that would be P(female | Sports).

options.label: D
options.feedbackWrong: 10/50 is the probability that a male student chose Sports, not female.

reteachModules.trigger: Student incorrectly calculates theoretical probability in discrete sample space scenarios.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Student fails to correctly identify the number of favorable outcomes and total outcomes in a discrete sample space with equally likely outcomes.

miniLesson.explain: Theoretical probability is the ratio of the number of favorable outcomes to the total number of equally likely outcomes in a discrete sample space. The formula is: P(event) = (number of favorable outcomes) / (total number of outcomes). Always ensure all outcomes are equally likely and count them correctly.
miniLesson.example: Roll a standard 6-sided die: probability of rolling a 4 is 1/6 because there is 1 favorable outcome (rolling a 4) out of 6 total possible outcomes.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Favorable over Total – that's the theoretical total!

guidedPractice.prompt: What is the probability of drawing a heart from a standard 52-card deck?
What is the probability of rolling an even number on a 6-sided die?
What is the probability of rolling a number less than 3 on a 6-sided die?

reteachModules.trigger: The student struggles to correctly identify regions in a three-set Venn diagram and compute probabilities such as P(exactly one set), P(union), P(intersection), or P(complement).
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Students often misinterpret the Venn diagram regions, for example counting students in 'only one set' as including those in intersections, or forgetting to include the 'none' region in the total sample space.

miniLesson.explain: A three-set Venn diagram divides the sample space into 8 regions: three individual sets (A only, B only, C only), three pairwise intersections (A∩B only, A∩C only, B∩C only), one triple intersection (A∩B∩C), and the complement (none of them). To find the probability of an event, sum the counts in all regions that satisfy the event, then divide by the total number of subjects (including those in none).
miniLesson.example: Consider a survey of after-school club participation: Sports (S), Music (M), Art (A). Counts: S only 13, M only 3, A only 4, S∩M only 6, S∩A only 4, M∩A only 2, all three 1, none 5. Total = 38. To find the probability a student is in exactly one club, sum the counts for S only (13), M only (3), A only (4) to get 20. So P = 20/38 = 10/19.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Think of a Venn diagram as a pizza with 8 slices. Each slice is a unique combination of toppings. To get probability, count the slices you want and divide by the whole pizza (including the 'none' slice).

guidedPractice.prompt: In the after-school club survey (Sports, Music, Art) with total 38 students, the counts are: S only 13, M only 3, A only 4, S∩M only 6, S∩A only 4, M∩A only 2, all three 1, none 5. What is the probability that a randomly selected student is in only Sports?
Using the same Venn diagram, what is the probability that a student is in exactly two clubs?
Using the same Venn diagram, what is the probability that a student is in at least two clubs?

reteachModules.trigger: Student incorrectly determines mutual exclusivity for events that share a common outcome, e.g., a card being both a heart and a king.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Students often think that events from different categories (e.g., suit vs rank) are automatically mutually exclusive because they are 'different' types, ignoring that a single outcome can belong to both events if it satisfies both conditions. They fail to check the intersection probability.

miniLesson.explain: Two events are mutually exclusive if they cannot happen at the same time. This means their intersection is empty: P(A∩B)=0. To check, ask: Can both events occur in a single trial? If yes, they are not mutually exclusive.
miniLesson.example: Drawing a heart and drawing a king from a deck: There is one card that is both (king of hearts), so P(A∩B)=1/52. Since this is not zero, the events are not mutually exclusive.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Think of a Venn diagram: if the circles overlap even a tiny bit, they are NOT mutually exclusive. Only when they are completely separate (no overlap) are they mutually exclusive.

guidedPractice.prompt: From a standard 52-card deck, are events 'drawing a red card' and 'drawing a club' mutually exclusive?
guidedPractice.answer: Yes, because a club is always black, so no overlap. P(A∩B)=0.

guidedPractice.prompt: From a standard 52-card deck, let A = drawing a face card (Jack, Queen, King) and B = drawing a heart. Are they mutually exclusive?
guidedPractice.answer: No, because there are three face cards that are hearts: Jack of Hearts, Queen of Hearts, King of Hearts. So P(A∩B)=3/52.

guidedPractice.prompt: Roll a 6-sided die. Let A = rolling an even number, B = rolling a number greater than 4. Are A and B mutually exclusive?
guidedPractice.answer: No, because 6 is both even and greater than 4, so they are not mutually exclusive. P(A∩B)=1/6.

questions.stem: A card is drawn from a standard 52-card deck. Let event A be 'drawing a face card' and event B be 'drawing a heart'. Are these events mutually exclusive?
options: Yes, because they are different categories
No, because there are cards that are both face cards and hearts
No, because P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A ∩ B)

questions.stem: A standard 6-sided die is rolled once. Let event C be 'rolling a number less than 3' and event D be 'rolling an odd number'. Determine whether events C and D are mutually exclusive. Show your reasoning.
questions.rubric: Student must compute P(C∩D): outcomes that are less than 3 and odd are {1}, so P=1/6 ≠ 0, thus not mutually exclusive. Equivalent correct reasoning accepted.

retestCards.passRule: All questions must be answered correctly. For the open-ended question, the answer must show correct reasoning that the events are not mutually exclusive because the intersection is non-empty.

What is the probability that a student who is female chose Sports?
cards.diagnosis: Check if student can compute a conditional probability by correctly restricting the sample space to the condition (female).
misconceptions: ✓ Correct. There are 100 females total, and 30 of them chose Sports.
30/150 would be the probability that a random student is female and chose Sports, not the conditional probability given female.
30/40 uses total number of students who chose Sports (40) as denominator; that would be P(female | Sports).
10/50 is the probability that a male student chose Sports, not female.
cards.successCriteria: Student correctly identifies the base (all females) and calculates 30/100.
cards.ossdExpectation: Determine the theoretical probability, Pi (i.e., a value from 0 to 1), of each outcome of a discrete sample space (e.g., in situations in which all outcomes are equally likely), recognize that the sum of the probabilities of the outcomes is 1 (i.e., for n outcomes, P1 + P2 + P3 + … + Pn = 1), recognize that the probabilities Pi form the probability distribution associated with the sample space, and solve related problems.
cards.alignmentNote: Conditional probability here requires theoretical probability from a subset of the sample space, aligning with SE A1.3.
cards.commonMisconception: Student uses total sample space as denominator (150) or uses the intersection of female and sports over total sports (30/40).
